title: The Richest Man in Rome, on Needing Nothing
author: Seneca
field: Stoic ethics and the use of time
wiifm: Seneca wrote the most beautiful Latin ever written about not needing money, while being one of the richest men in Rome and the chief adviser to Nero. We follow him from a sickly boy in Spain, through eight years of exile on Corsica and into the most dangerous job in the empire, to a villa outside Rome where soldiers arrived with orders. On the way you get his ideas on time as the only asset you truly own, rehearsing hardship, choosing your company and grieving well, plus a working case study in how a clever man lives with a compromise.

b: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born around 4 BC in Córdoba, in the Roman province of southern Spain, the second of three sons in a rich family of the equestrian class. His father, also Lucius, was a wealthy man obsessed with public speaking, who in old age wrote down from memory the speeches of the great declaimers he had heard. We call him Seneca the Elder to keep them apart.

The boy was taken to Rome when he was very small, apparently carried there by an aunt, and was educated in rhetoric and then, to his father's mild disapproval, in philosophy. He fell hard for it. As a young man he gave up meat for a year on the advice of a teacher and found his mind sharper for it, until his father, nervous that odd diets might look like membership of a foreign cult, asked him to stop. Seneca tells this story himself, years later, in one of his letters.

He was also ill, badly and for a long time, with what seems to have been asthma or a chronic chest disease. In another letter he admits that as a young man he thought of ending his life, and was held back only by the thought that his old father would not bear it. In his twenties he went to Egypt, where his aunt's husband was governor, partly to recover, and he came back to Rome around 31 AD to begin a political career.

Keep two things from this beginning: a body that never let him forget he was mortal, and a father who loved words. Seneca would become the most quotable prose writer in Latin, and he would write about death more than about anything except time.
ch.cap: An aunt carries little Seneca from Córdoba toward Rome

b: His career rose quickly, and so did the danger. He became a celebrated speaker in the Senate. Cassius Dio, writing well over a century later, claims the Emperor Caligula was so jealous of one of his speeches that he ordered him killed, and spared him only because someone said he was sickly and would die soon anyway. Dio loves a story, so hold that one loosely.

Under the next emperor, Claudius, the danger became real. In 41 AD Seneca was accused of adultery with Julia Livilla, the dead Caligula's sister, very probably at the prompting of Claudius's wife Messalina, and he was banished to Corsica. He stayed for eight years.

Exile produced two very different pieces of writing. One was a consolation to his mother, Helvia, telling her not to grieve for him, because a wise man is at home anywhere and fortune cannot take away what fortune never gave. It is noble and it is Stoic. The other was a consolation to Polybius, a powerful freedman of Claudius whose brother had died. Under the cover of comforting him, it flatters Claudius shamelessly and hints how wonderful it would be to be called home.

That pairing is the whole of Seneca in miniature. The same man, in the same years, on the same island, wrote the doctrine and wrote the grovelling letter. When the recall finally came in 49, it was not Claudius who sent for him. It was Claudius's new wife, Agrippina, who wanted a famous tutor for her young son. The boy's name was Nero.
ch.cap: Exiled on Corsica, Seneca writes two very different letters

b: In 54 Claudius died, almost certainly poisoned, and Nero became emperor at sixteen. Seneca wrote the speeches the young emperor delivered at the start of his reign. He also wrote, for the amusement of the court, a savage satire on the dead Claudius called the Apocolocyntosis, roughly the pumpkinification, in which the late emperor tries and fails to become a god.

For the next several years Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus effectively steered the empire, and later Romans looked back on the early part of Nero's reign as good government. Within months, though, Nero's stepbrother Britannicus collapsed at dinner and died, almost certainly poisoned. Shortly afterwards Seneca wrote On Clemency, a treatise on mercy addressed to the young emperor, praising him for having shed no blood and urging him to make mercy his glory.
You can read that as courage, an adviser trying to bind a dangerous young man to a public ideal. You can read it as cover. Both readings have their defenders, and both are probably partly true.

Meanwhile Seneca was becoming staggeringly rich: gifts from the emperor, estates in Italy and Egypt, fine villas, and large sums lent at interest. In 58 a hostile senator named Publius Suillius demanded to know by what kind of wisdom Seneca had made three hundred million sesterces in four years of imperial friendship. Suillius was an enemy and the figure is partisan. Nobody disputes that Seneca was one of the wealthiest men in Rome.
ch.cap: Seneca hands young Nero a speech on mercy

b: In 59 Nero had his own mother murdered. Agrippina survived a collapsing boat designed to drown her, and was then killed by soldiers at her villa. According to the historian Tacitus, Seneca and Burrus were consulted, and it was Seneca who was believed to have drafted the letter Nero sent to the Senate, claiming she had plotted against him and killed herself when caught. Even at the time, Tacitus says, people blamed Seneca for writing a confession dressed up as a speech.

There is a darker rumour still. In 60 or 61 the Iceni of Britain rose under Boudica and burned Colchester, London and St Albans. Tacitus gives the causes as the flogging of Boudica, the rape of her daughters and the seizure of land. Cassius Dio, writing much later, adds one more: that Seneca had lent the British nobility forty million sesterces they had not wanted, and then called the whole sum in at once and harshly. Dio is late and hostile and the claim cannot be checked. But it is in the record.

In 62 Burrus died and Seneca's position crumbled. He asked Nero for permission to retire and offered to hand back his fortune. Nero embraced him and refused both. Seneca withdrew anyway, as far as he dared, stopped receiving crowds of visitors, and spent his time writing. He asked again in 64, after the Great Fire of Rome, and was refused again.

So here is the question that has followed him for two thousand years. How do you read a man who wrote the finest Latin on contempt for wealth while lending at interest, and the finest Latin on moral courage while drafting cover for a mother's murder? Keep it open. The answer comes at the end, and it is not the obvious one.
ch.cap: As Agrippina's boat collapses, Seneca drafts the cover story

b: In those last years of uneasy retirement Seneca wrote his masterpiece: one hundred and twenty-four surviving letters, in twenty books, to a younger friend called Lucilius, a real man from a modest background who had risen to be the emperor's financial officer in Sicily. Whether the letters were ever actually sent is debated. They read like a planned course in living well, dressed as correspondence, and Seneca clearly expected them to be published.

Each letter takes one ordinary situation, a noisy flat above a bathhouse, a visit to his old country house, an attack of asthma, a voyage that left him seasick, and draws one usable idea from it in a few pages. He writes in short, punchy sentences that grander Roman stylists found almost vulgar. He is writing for busy people, and there is still no better model for turning a small concrete irritation into a principle without padding.

The very first letter is about time. Everything else, he tells Lucilius, belongs to others. Time alone is ours. We guard money and property, which can be replaced, and hand out hours to anyone who asks, which cannot. In his essay On the Shortness of Life he goes further and rejects the familiar complaint itself. Life is not short, he says. We make it short by wasting it. It is long enough if you know how to use it.

His word for the busy man is occupatus, occupied, the word used of a city taken by an enemy. The man rushing between duties he never chose owns no more of his life than a man asleep. He is scathing about people who plan to start living properly once they retire, postponing the only thing that is truly theirs. And in the second letter, warning Lucilius against skipping between too many books, he gives a line that applies far beyond reading: to be everywhere is to be nowhere.
ch.cap: Above a noisy bathhouse, Seneca writes about time

b: Letter 18 is written in December, during the Saturnalia, when Rome gave itself over to feasting, gifts and licence. Seneca's advice is stranger than either joining the party or sulking above it. Set aside a few days, he tells Lucilius, and live on the scantiest and cheapest food, in rough, coarse clothing. Then ask yourself: is this what I used to fear?

The point is not to look holy. Seneca is clear that he does not want Lucilius to become one of those men who make a show of shabby clothes and unkempt hair. The point is to take a measurement. Much of the fear that governs a comfortable person's choices is fear of a condition they have never tested. Test it, and you find the floor is far higher than you imagined. Plain food is edible. A hard bed can be slept in. The fear loses its grip on your decisions. It is in times of safety, he writes, that the mind should prepare itself for hard times.

Here his wealth becomes evidence rather than embarrassment. He is not a poor man making a virtue of necessity. He is a rich man choosing poverty for a few days, precisely so that the riches stop owning him.

He applies the same thinking to possessions in general. Enjoy them, but hold them as borrowed, the way a careful man looks after money that belongs to someone else. The test of whether you have got this right is not how little you own. It is how you behave in the week after you lose some of it. For a business, the equivalent is an austerity week once a year, with no new spending, no paid advertising and no new hires, simply to find out where the floor really is. Most owners have never seen it, and so they negotiate from imagined weakness.
ch.cap: While Rome feasts, rich Seneca rehearses poverty

ch.h: Coming home worse from the games
b: Letter 7 begins with a confession. Seneca happened to drop in on the midday show at the arena, hoping for some wit and relaxation. Instead he found the interval entertainment: condemned men sent out to kill each other without armour, plain butchery, while the crowd shouted for more. He came home, he says, more greedy, more ambitious, more cruel and less humane, because he had been among people.

His conclusion is severe. Nothing is so damaging to good character as sitting in a crowd at a spectacle, because vice slips in more easily through pleasure. We are not argued into a crowd's values. We soak them up through exposure, and fastest when we are enjoying ourselves. So withdraw into yourself as much as you can, he tells Lucilius, spend time with people who will make you better, and welcome those whom you can improve. It runs both ways, he adds. People learn while they teach.

This is not hatred of people. It is a claim about direction of travel. In every room you sit in regularly, your character is moving one way or the other, and the honest question about any group chat, trade association or Friday drinks is which way it is moving yours.

Letter 47 turns the same humane eye on slavery. Seneca attacks the Roman habit of treating household slaves as furniture, forced to stand silent all evening and beaten for a cough. They are slaves, he says. No, they are human beings. Fortune has the same power over both of you, he reminds Lucilius, and he urges him to eat with his slaves. It is one of the most humane documents from the ancient world. It was also written by a man who owned a great many slaves, with no record that he freed them. Reading Seneca means holding both facts at once.
ch.cap: At the midday games, Seneca recoils from the butchery

b: Seneca is better on grief than almost anyone, because he refuses both easy positions. In Letter 63, written after the death of Lucilius's friend Flaccus, he grants at once that tears are natural. A man who feels nothing has not reached wisdom. He has lost something human.

But he also makes the Stoic case against endless mourning. We weep partly to be seen weeping. We are often more afraid of looking unfeeling than we are actually sad. The useful question is whether your grief honours the dead or performs for the living. And he confesses, with real candour, that when his own dear friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept so uncontrollably that he became an example of the very thing he warns against.

His remedy is strange and it works. Treat the friends you have lost as something lent to you and now returned, and let the memory become a pleasure rather than a wound, the way some old wines carry a pleasant bitterness. Then draw the obvious conclusion for the living. If you will one day be glad to have known them, be glad now, while they are still here. Let us enjoy our friends greedily, he says, because we do not know how long we will have them.
ch.cap: Seneca and Lucilius drink to friends, beside an empty chair

b: In April 65 a plot to kill Nero, led by the senator Gaius Calpurnius Piso, was betrayed. Most historians doubt that Seneca was really part of it, but he was named, and that was enough. Soldiers surrounded his villa four miles outside Rome, and a centurion delivered the order to die.

Tacitus, writing about fifty years later, tells the rest. Seneca asked for his will so that he could change it, and was refused. So he turned to his friends and said that since he was forbidden to repay their kindness, he would leave them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the pattern of his life. His wife Paulina insisted on dying with him, and they opened their veins together.

His body would not cooperate. He was old and thin from his frugal diet, and the blood came slowly. He took hemlock, the poison of Socrates, and it did not work. Nero, who did not want to be blamed for Paulina's death, ordered her wounds to be bound, and she lived for some years afterwards. In the end Seneca was carried into a hot bath and suffocated by the steam.

Tacitus clearly relished this scene, and he may have polished it. But the core is not in dispute. The man who had written so much about how to die was given a long, messy afternoon to do it in front of others, and by every account we have, he did not disgrace himself.
ch.cap: Soldiers wait as Seneca dies in the steam bath

b: So, back to the question. How should you read the rich man who preached poverty and the courtier who preached courage?

The lazy answer is that he was a hypocrite and the work is worthless. That confuses the author's report card with the truth of the argument. Whether time is our only real possession does not depend on how well Seneca spent his. The kinder answer, which his admirers prefer, is that he was a philosopher trapped beside a monster, doing what harm reduction he could. That has some force. He says again and again that he is not a wise man, only one trying to get better. In one letter he describes himself as lying in the same hospital ward as his reader, talking about the illness they share, rather than handing down a cure.

The most useful answer goes further. Seneca matters precisely because he failed in the ordinary way. He wanted the money, took the job, flattered the man he should have opposed, knew it, and wrote about it beautifully anyway. That puts him inside the gap between knowing and doing, which is exactly where the rest of us live.

So read him with the case against him kept open. You get a double education: a set of tools for living, and a working case study in how a very intelligent person explains away a compromise he has already made. Both are worth having.
ch.cap: Seneca talks from his sickbed beside his reader's

take: You defend money that can be replaced and give away hours that cannot. Treat a request for an hour with the scrutiny you would give a request for cash.

Go through last month's diary and mark each item as chosen for a reason you can state, or inherited because it was already there. Cancel three inherited items this week and see what breaks; usually nothing does.
A few days of plain living, or an austerity week in the business, is a measurement, not a virtue. Once you have stood on the floor you stop negotiating from imagined weakness.
Hold what you own as borrowed
Enjoy possessions with the care of someone managing another person's money. The test is how you behave in the week after you lose some.
Values are absorbed through exposure and pleasure, not argument. Ask which way each regular group in your life moves your work, and quietly reduce time with the one that drags you down.
Feeling nothing is not wisdom, and endless mourning is partly performance. If you will one day be glad to have known someone, be glad now, and call them.
Seneca's advice survives his failures because he never claimed to be cured, only under treatment. Speak about your own standards the same way and you become harder to dismiss.
Separate the author from the argument
He did not live up to it settles nothing about whether an idea is true. Use the argument, keep the case against the author open, and learn how clever people dress up compromises.
recall: What does Seneca say instead of life is short, and what word does he use for the busy man?

Life is not short; we make it short by wasting it, guarding replaceable money while giving away hours that cannot be replaced. His word for the busy man is occupatus, occupied like a city taken by an enemy, a man not in possession of his own life.
What is the exercise in Letter 18, and what is it for?

During the Saturnalia, spend a few days on the cheapest food and roughest clothing, then ask whether this is what you feared. It is a measurement rather than a virtue: it shows the floor is far higher than imagined, so the fear stops governing your choices.
What happened to Seneca at the arena in Letter 7, and what did he conclude?

He came home greedier, more ambitious and crueller than he went. He concluded that vice is absorbed through exposure and pleasure rather than argument, so you should spend time with people who will improve you and welcome those you can improve.
Give three items in the case against Seneca's character.

Any three of: Suillius's charge that he made three hundred million sesterces in four years; Dio's claim that calling in loans to British nobles helped provoke Boudica's revolt; drafting Nero's letter justifying Agrippina's murder; flattering Claudius from exile and mocking him once dead; owning many slaves while writing Letter 47.
How did Seneca die, and how reliable is the account?

Ordered to die after the Pisonian conspiracy of 65, he opened his veins with his wife Paulina, took hemlock without effect, and was finally suffocated in a hot bath; Paulina was saved on Nero's orders. The account is Tacitus's, written about fifty years later and probably polished, but the core facts are not disputed.
note: Main sources are Seneca's own letters and essays, Tacitus's Annals for Suillius's charge, the letter after Agrippina's murder, the retirement requests and the death scene, and Cassius Dio for the Caligula story and the British loans. Dio is late and hostile and the Boudica claim cannot be verified; Tacitus's death scene is probably polished, and Seneca's part in the Agrippina letter is reported as belief rather than proof. His birth year is approximate, and whether the letters were really sent is debated.
words: Servile flattery of a powerful person in the hope of gaining favour.
From exile on Corsica Seneca wrote a consolation to Claudius's freedman Polybius that slides into sycophancy towards the emperor, hinting how lovely a recall would be.
Lending money at interest, especially at high or exploitative rates.
Seneca praised contempt for wealth while lending large sums at interest, and Cassius Dio, a late and hostile source, blamed his harsh loan recall in Britain for helping provoke Boudica's revolt.
The killing of one's own mother.
After Nero's matricide in 59, Seneca was believed to have drafted the letter to the Senate claiming Agrippina had plotted and killed herself.
Extreme poverty, lacking even basic necessities.
In Letter 18 Seneca tells Lucilius to rehearse penury for a few days, cheap food and coarse clothes, and ask whether this is what he used to fear.
Clever but unsound reasoning used to justify a doubtful action.
Reading Seneca gives a case study in casuistry, a brilliant mind explaining away compromises he had already made, though he also admitted he was a patient rather than a doctor.
stories: In 41 AD Seneca was accused of adultery with the emperor Caligula's sister, very probably at the prompting of the empress Messalina, and banished to Corsica for eight years. From that island he wrote two famous pieces. One, to his mother, told her not to grieve, because a wise man is at home anywhere and fortune cannot take what it never gave. The other, to a powerful freedman of the emperor Claudius, flattered Claudius shamelessly and hinted how wonderful it would be to come home. Same man, same years, same island. When the recall came, it was Agrippina who sent for him, to tutor her son. His name was Nero.
Coming home worse from the games

One lunchtime Seneca dropped in at the arena hoping for a bit of wit and relaxation between the main shows. Instead he found the interval entertainment: condemned men sent out without armour to kill each other while the crowd yelled for more. He went home, he told his friend Lucilius, more greedy, more ambitious, more cruel and less humane, because he had been among people. His point was not that people are bad. It was that nobody argues you into a crowd's values. You soak them up, fastest when you are enjoying yourself, so choose the rooms you sit in on purpose.
The death that would not come

In April 65 a plot to kill Nero was betrayed and Seneca was named, though most historians doubt he was really involved. Soldiers surrounded his villa outside Rome and a centurion delivered the order to die. According to Tacitus, who may have polished the scene, Seneca told his friends that since he could not repay them, he would leave them the pattern of his life. He and his wife Paulina opened their veins. His thin old body bled too slowly. He took hemlock, the poison of Socrates, and it failed. In the end he was carried into a hot bath and suffocated by the steam. He did not disgrace himself.
biz: Find your floor before you need it

Seneca rehearsed poverty so that fear of it stopped running his choices. You do not need to switch off paid ads to do the same. Once a quarter, model a month with no Google, Bing or Facebook spend using real numbers: how many enquiries arrive from SEO, direct traffic, referrals and returning customers, and what that pays in procuration fees after costs. Write the figure down. Owners who have never seen their floor negotiate with lenders, agencies and suppliers from imagined weakness. Track the organic share of completed cases monthly; if it is rising, the floor is rising, and your decisions can get calmer and fairer.
Choose the company your leads keep

Seneca came home worse from the arena because standards are absorbed, not argued. The same happens with lead sources. If you buy or share leads, or sit in industry groups where pushy tactics are normal, those habits drift into your own scripts. This week, list every lead source and partner and score each on three things: complaint rate, how often the customer did not remember enquiring, and how many show signs of vulnerability that were not flagged. Drop or retrain any source that brings you distressed people through aggressive copy. Under Consumer Duty you own the outcomes of the customers you accept, wherever they came from.
connects: Seneca's rich man choosing poverty for a few days to stop his money owning him is the ancient version of Housel's argument that the real return on wealth is not needing more of it.
Seneca's warning that the occupied man owns none of his life, and that to be everywhere is to be nowhere, is the moral core of Newport's case for protecting long uninterrupted hours.
Both Seneca and Machiavelli were clever advisers trying to steer a dangerous ruler, and both raise the question of how much compromise a man can make in power before the advice becomes cover.
recap:
Seneca was born in Córdoba, in Roman Spain, a little before the Christian era began, into a rich family with a father who adored fine speaking. He grew up sickly, with a chest that never let him forget he was mortal, and he fell hard for philosophy. He rose fast in Rome, and the danger rose with him. In the year forty-one he was accused of adultery with the late emperor's sister and exiled to Corsica for eight years. There he wrote a noble letter to his mother about how a wise man is at home anywhere, and a grovelling one to a court favourite begging to come home. That pairing is the whole man.

He was recalled to tutor a boy called Nero. When Nero became emperor, Seneca effectively helped run the empire, grew staggeringly rich, lent money at interest, and was believed to have drafted the letter that covered up Nero's murder of his own mother. Twice he asked to retire and hand back his fortune. Twice Nero refused.

In those last uneasy years he wrote his masterpiece, a long series of letters to a younger friend, Lucilius, and here are the ideas worth keeping.

First, time is the only thing truly yours. We guard money, which can be replaced, and give away hours, which cannot. Life is not short. We make it short by wasting it.

Second, rehearse hardship. For a few days, live on cheap food and rough clothing and ask whether this is what you were afraid of. The floor is higher than you think, and once you have seen it, fear stops making your decisions.

Third, choose your company. Seneca came home from the arena crueller than he went, because we soak up a crowd's values without noticing.

Fourth, grieve well. Tears are human. But enjoy your friends greedily now, because you do not know how long you will have them.

In the year sixty-five he was ordered to die. His body would not cooperate, and the end was long and messy, but by every account he met it with dignity.

So was he a hypocrite? In part, yes. But whether time is our only real possession does not depend on how well Seneca spent his. He called himself a patient, not a doctor, lying in the same ward as his reader.

The line to remember: nothing is ours except time.
